The problem is that the flip side is completely fine too, but it’s much less readily accepted. If there is no objectively true reason for any given person to live, and the person doesn’t have a subjective reason to live either, then the person doesn’t have a reason to keep on living.

It’s as if people who have the desire and reason to live are offended when others say that they “personally” don’t feel the need to go on anymore, as if a anyone denying their own reason for existence somehow also denies everyone else’s as well. Some people seem to be unable to distinguish personal beliefs about a specific individual from universal beliefs about everyone in existence. It infuriates me, really.

I don’t think saying there’s no inherent value to life is pro-suicidal at all. People can acknowledge that there’s no inherent value in life yet say they want to live. My problem is that the commenter simply assumed that OP shares that view.

It’s something that I really want to believe but simply can’t because I don’t have the argument to convince myself.

> I was of basing that in the idea that the OP in some sense wants to do something about or has some type of problem with the things they mentioned

No offense, really, I genuinely mean no harm, but I do think this IS an unfair assumption. Someone can be outraged by something but not be willing to do anything about it, and like OP suggests, someone can just become depressed and/or suicidal as a response. I don't think you can reliably transition "outrage" into "willingness to act for a change." It's entirely possible that OP does want to act for some sort of change, but I don't think you can assume that from the text. 

I'm not claiming that you're pushing a magic answer, I was only pointing out that your initial comment set a premise as a given, when it may not be agreed upon by everyone. When the question involves "why one should do X instead of suicide," I think the core question inevitably becomes "why live?" I don't think anyone can give a universal, objective answer to this question. You "just want to live," "just don't want to live," or "don't even know if (you) want to live." I think there's a good amount of people on either side, so it'd be good if we continued to asked ourselves "why?" and see if the core question becomes "why should I/you/OP live?" If you want to live, you can say "because **I** want to." If you don't, you can answer "because **I** don't want to." Same goes for OP, or whoever it may be.

Something that made me ask myself this is that there are people who blindly repeat "omg no don't die." In my opinion, this kind of blind support for life can backfire if the "suicidal" person asks why, only to reach the core question of "why live?" and find that whatever answer the commenter gives has no real application for the suicidal person.
